title: Sentence Stems: A Practical AI Guide
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews offers a practical guide to using AI to generate context-specific sentence stems -- a writing scaffold that provides the beginning of a sentence for students to complete. The piece explains the theory: sentence stems sit in the Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky) by providing just enough structure to enable independent completion without doing the intellectual work for the student. They work for both single-blank stems (one clear completion) and multi-blank stems (multiple possible completions that require genuine thinking to populate correctly). Matthews then walks through a workflow for using AI to generate high-quality, subject-specific stems: providing the AI with the specific topic, the learning objective, the student's current level, and examples of what good and poor completions would look like. The piece includes worked examples from multiple subjects and grade levels, and addresses the common failure mode of generic stems ('The author uses _____ to ___') that can be completed without the target thinking.
points: * Sentence stems function as Zone of Proximal Development scaffolds (Vygotsky): they provide just enough structure to enable independent completion while requiring the student to do the genuine cognitive work of populating the stem. * AI is particularly well-suited to generating context-specific sentence stems because it can be given the exact topic, objective, and student level needed, producing stems that are pedagogically calibrated rather than generically applicable. * Multi-blank stems require more thinking than single-blank stems and are more resistant to thoughtless completion: 'The author uses _____ to show that _____, which suggests that _____' forces a chain of reasoning rather than a single word. * The common failure mode is generic stems ('The author uses _____ to _____') that can be completed without engaging with the specific text or topic -- context-specific stems require the student to draw on the actual content. * Matthews' AI workflow includes four elements: specific topic, learning objective, student level, and examples of good and poor completions -- the last being the most important for calibrating the AI's output to the right level of difficulty.
quotes: A sentence stem is not training wheels. It is a scaffold -- a temporary support that enables the student to do work they couldn't do without it, while the work itself develops the capacity to do it without the scaffold. That's the Vygotsky logic, and it's why stems are a more pedagogically defensible tool than 'just give them the answer.'

The problem with most sentence stems is that they're too generic to require genuine thinking. 'The author uses _____ to _____' can be completed by a student who has not read the text at all. The power of context-specific stems is that they require the student to draw on the specific content to complete them correctly.

AI can generate context-specific stems at a quality level and speed that would take a teacher thirty minutes per lesson to match. The workflow is: give the AI the topic, the objective, the student level, and an example of what a thoughtful completion would look like. The AI produces stems. You choose the best ones.

Multi-blank stems are the most powerful variety. 'The evidence shows _____, which suggests that _____, but this interpretation is challenged by _____' requires a chain of reasoning. The student who fills all three blanks correctly has done the analytical work of the lesson. The blank is not the thinking. It is the occasion for thinking.

The failure mode to watch for is stems that can be completed by any sufficiently fluent student regardless of whether they understand the content. 'The character felt _____ because _____' is a generic emotional observation. 'Gatsby's decision to throw parties suggests he believes _____, which reveals that his real motivation is _____' is content-specific analysis. AI can generate either. Your job is to prompt for the latter.
